extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government / general readers seeking background on U.S. civil service and Congress
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes statutory and administrative standards governing federal civil service examinations, appointments, promotion, removal, political-activity restrictions, and provisions and practices governing the House of Representatives (membership qualifications, apportionment, districting, gerrymandering, and term length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical character of civil service examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations shall be "practical in their character, and, so far as may be, relate to those matters which will fairly test the relative capacity and fitness of persons examined to discharge the duties" of the branch of the government service to which they seek admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission asks cooperation of departments; if a technical position is to be filled, the department usually prepares the technical questions. Examinations should test capacities and fitness relevant to the duties of the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenient and inexpensive exam locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards of examiners shall be erected at such points as to make it reasonably convenient and inexpensive for applicants to attend examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a chief examiner in Washington and several hundred local boards scattered among the states and territories for supervising local examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of positions and exam divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Positions covered by the merit system are classified into groups arranged by salary and for examining purposes separated into six divisions: clerical, technical, executive, mechanical, sub-clerical, and miscellaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About two-thirds of federal offices covered are clerical; technical/professional positions are a smaller share. Classification guides the content and design of exam papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open eligibility to citizens and grounds for exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any citizen of the United States may apply for an examination, but citizens are excluded on grounds such as mental or physical incapacity, excessive use of intoxicants, service in the army or navy, dismissal from public service for delinquency during the preceding year, and criminal or disgraceful conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizenship requirement has been more rigidly enforced in recent years; the statute lists specific disqualifying conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No applicant fees (but consideration of nominal charge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants for examination are not charged a fee, though the Civil Service Commission has recommended a nominal charge to discourage ill-prepared persons who take exams in a gambling spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nominal fee would serve to exclude those with nothing to lose and thus reduce frivolous applicants; currently exams are free to applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of registers of eligibles to cover diverse needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Civil Service Commission must keep its registers of eligibles full so it can supply men of the most diverse training and experience when called upon by departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registers allow immediate supply of clerks, stenographers, chemists, patent examiners, draftsmen, interpreters, postal clerks, etc., as demands arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection procedure — transmission of three candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: When called upon, the Commission selects from the proper register and transmits to the department the names of three candidates at the head of the list, who are, if possible, residents of the state wherein the appointment falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this list of three any one may be selected by the appointing officer; the other names are returned to the Commission to be replaced on the register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to justify refusal of Commission candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: If the appointing officer refuses to accept any one of the three names transmitted by the Commission, he must give satisfactory reasons for his action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This imposes an accountability requirement on appointing officers who decline recommended eligibles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probationary period for appointees
rubrics_metrics.description: Every successful candidate is put on probation for a period of six months; if his record is good his appointment is made permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probation is the standard means of determining final fitness for permanent appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference and exemptions in appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain exceptions exist: (1) preference is given to persons honorably discharged from military or naval service; (2) persons nominated for confirmation by the Senate need not be classified or pass an examination; (3) private secretaries to department heads, assistants, bureau chiefs, attorneys, and persons in emergency employments are generally exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long printed list of specific exemptions exists in Civil Service Reports; in practice many higher or political offices are excluded from competitive classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of Washington department appointments (statutory principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments to the public service in the departments at Washington shall be apportioned among the several states and territories and the District of Columbia upon the basis of population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes this is a principle difficult to carry out in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and process for removal from competitive service
rubrics_metrics.description: No person shall be removed from a competitive position except for such causes as will promote the efficiency of the service; the President or head of an executive department, when convinced any employee is incapable or inefficient, may remove such employee without notice. A department head may, at his discretion, require that notice be given and a reasonable time afforded for answering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally do not interfere with removals; removal power is viewed as tied to appointment power. Department heads carry responsibility for efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Service Act limit on removal for political refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Civil Service Act limits the power of removal in one instance — refusal to contribute money or service to a political party (i.e., employees shall not be removed or prejudiced for refusing to contribute to political funds or services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, widespread removals of employees of the same political faith create a presumption of political motive and require justification, though courts rarely intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required efficiency records and their use
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative officers are required to keep 'efficiency records' of employees and render periodical reports giving records in diligence, punctuality, faithfulness, and accuracy; these records are filed and used as the basis for promotion or expulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system is criticized for subjectivity and encouraging servility and pretense, but is defended as a deterrent to negligence; no mechanical rating can reveal real capacities but some record-keeping seems indispensable for promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion procedures and supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The law makes provision for promotions; competitive examinations are established to test fitness of candidates for promotion and a list of eligibles for advancement is kept; candidates may use recommendations from chiefs to support their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotions combine objective (exams, registers) and subjective (recommendations, efficiency records) elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on active partisan political activity for classified employees
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons in the competitive classified service, while retaining the right to vote and express private opinions, 'shall take no active part in political management or in political campaigns.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission interpreted this to forbid: service on political committees; service as delegates to county/state/district conventions (with caveats); continued political leadership; publication of a newspaper in interest of a political party; membership in clubs taking active part in campaigns; circulation of petitions with a political object; service as commissioner of elections in communities where the commissioner is necessarily an active politician.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on coercion and solicitation of political assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: No person in the public service has a right to use his authority to coerce the political action of any person. Members of Congress and executive, judicial, military, and naval officers are forbidden to be involved in soliciting or receiving political assistance or contributions from any officer employed by the United States or from any person receiving compensation from the United States. Soliciting campaign contributions in federal buildings is likewise forbidden by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prohibitions are intended to separate official authority from partisan fundraising and pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern and provision for superannuation/retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of permanent tenure raises the question of what to do with employees past the age of efficient service; it is argued that provision for retirement (civil pensions) is the practical solution to superannuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retiring older, inefficient men would open promotion opportunities for younger able men and improve administration; President Taft advocated civil pensions as practical remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: House membership constitutional qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of the House must be a citizen of the United States for at least seven years, at least twenty-five years old, and an inhabitant of the state in which chosen; he cannot simultaneously be a military or civil officer of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States generally forbid their officers to hold federal trust positions; some states require district residency although most lawyers view such additions as unconstitutional qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: House power to judge qualifications and exclude members
rubrics_metrics.description: While states cannot add qualifications to those imposed by the federal Constitution, each house, in exercising its powers to judge elections, returns, and qualifications, may exclude persons on other grounds than those laid down in the Constitution (illustrated by the exclusion of Brigham H. Roberts for polygamy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is debate — minority view warned that adding disqualifications is unconstitutional and dangerous precedent; alternative remedy is admission then expulsion by two-thirds vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment and districting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are apportioned among the states by population (counting whole number of persons, exclusive of Indians not taxed); congressional districts are required to be composed of 'contiguous and compact territory containing as nearly as practicable an equal number of inhabitants,' each district electing only one Representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If state legislature fails to make districts as required, certain or all members may be elected at large on a general ticket. The Apportionment Act of 1842 established single-member contiguous districts as the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against gerrymandering and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Gerrymandering — the deliberate drawing of district lines for partisan advantage by packing opposition voters into few districts and spreading the dominant party's vote to win many districts by small margins — results in gross inequalities between votes cast and seats won.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and statistics illustrate how parties can secure disproportionate representation; the text treats gerrymandering as a misuse of districting power that distorts representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length and its administrative/political effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of a member of the House is two years. Short term criticized for causing members to devote attention to campaign for renomination/election, diverting energy from official duties and limiting influence because practical experience in procedure is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-year terms produce trade-offs: responsiveness versus continuity and effectiveness; there is no provision for dissolution of the House or recall of members.
